# **Design and Implementation of a WebGIS Architecture for Parcel Information Services in Lagos State, Nigeria**

**Abstract**

Land Information Services (LIServices) across developing nations continue to face systemic bottlenecks arising from manual record-keeping, fragmented spatial datasets, restricted public transparency, and limited interoperability. While a complete Land Information System (LIS) requires full-scale legal, administrative, and multi-agency institutional integration, production-grade client/server WebGIS interfaces offer an essential spatial foundation for digital parcel visualization, attribute retrieval, and multi-criteria spatial querying. This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of a decoupled, three-tier WebGIS architecture tailored for parcel information services in Lagos State, utilizing the Otedola Estate layout (471 parcels) as an empirical case study. The prototype—termed Land Information System and Services (LISAS)—transitions client-side storage approaches toward a robust enterprise geospatial stack: a PostgreSQL/PostGIS spatial database tier structured around the ISO 19152 Land Administration Domain Model (LADM) and Cadastre 2014/2034 principles, an asynchronous RESTful API backend tier, and a responsive Leaflet.js WebGIS presentation layer. System performance, execution latency, and usability were systematically evaluated over 30 test cycles across key operational scenarios alongside System Usability Scale (SUS) assessments. Results demonstrate sub-second query execution speeds (${\mu }_{search}=0.82$ s, ${\mu }_{map}=1.94$ s, ${\mu }_{query}=0.65$ s) with low coefficients of variation ($CV<20%$), statistically significant time savings over legacy physical registry processes ($t=18.72,p<0.001$), and an overall usability score of 82.5/100. This research provides a scalable, open-source technical blueprint for fit-for-purpose geospatial interface deployment in urban land administration.

# **1	Introduction**

Land Information Services (LIServices) in many developing countries, including Nigeria, continue to face severe operational challenges associated with legacy manual processes, fragmented spatial datasets, and limited system interoperability (**Adam, 2023**; **Rohan, 2023**). These structural constraints lead to administrative inefficiencies, transaction delays, revenue leakage, and a lack of public transparency in land governance (**Williamson, 2020**). Recent empirical studies emphasize that the absence of integrated digital spatial systems directly impacts public service delivery, land tenure security, and investor confidence (**Adam, 2023**). Modern Land Administration Systems (LAS) are increasingly shifting toward cloud-native, service-oriented architectures that seamlessly fuse spatial geometries with legal attributes to support sustainable development, economic growth, and transparent governance (**Williamson, 2020**; **Rohan, 2023**).

The rapid evolution of Web-based Geographic Information Systems (WebGIS) has transformed land information management by enabling real-time spatial visualization, asynchronous attribute querying, and public engagement in land governance (**Luong, 2025**). Concurrent advancements, notably the International Organization for Standardization’s Land Administration Domain Model (ISO 19152: LADM Edition I and Edition II) and the International Federation of Surveyors (FIG) Cadastre 2014/2034 visions, establish standardized conceptual frameworks for unifying legal, administrative, party, and spatial unit data (K**aufmann, 1998**; **Luthy, 2015**; **van Oosterom, 2025**). These frameworks stress technology adoption readiness, institutional alignment, and scalable architectural design, particularly within African urbanization contexts (**Duku, 2023**).

While complete enterprise Land Information Systems encompass multi-agency legal administration (e.g., automated deed registration, encumbrance tracking, digital signatures, and Governor’s consent workflows), a crucial component of modern land infrastructure is a lightweight, scalable, client/server WebGIS interface dedicated to parcel visualization, attribute retrieval, and spatial querying.

This paper presents the conceptual design, enterprise system architecture, data modeling, methodology, implementation, and empirical performance evaluation of a modern Web-based parcel service platform titled **Land Information System and Services (LISAS)** for Lagos State. Reframing initial client-centric storage models into a decoupled three-tier spatial architecture (PostgreSQL/PostGIS data tier, Python FastAPI middleware tier, and Leaflet.js frontend tier), this study demonstrates how open-source geospatial tools achieve high system stability, robust statistical convergence, sub-second execution response, and superior usability.

# **2	Architecture and Conceptual Framework**

## **2.1	LISAS System Architecture**

The proposed LISAS platform adopts a centralized, decoupled three-tier architecture illustrated conceptually in Figure [1](#bookmark=id.r4wcxuszj1lq). The architecture acts as a one-stop portal connecting internal government personnel within the Office of the State Surveyor-General (OSSG) and Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs), as well as external regular users (professionals, registered surveyors, financial institutions) and ad-hoc public users.

![][image1]

Figure 1: Decoupled LISAS Service Architecture and Stakeholder Interactions.

The Central Service Centre (CSC) functions as the core digital single-window. Ad-hoc and regular external users interact with the system via web browsers, mobile endpoints, and automated API channels.

## **2.2	Users’ Requirements Layering**

Land information service delivery depends on meeting structured stakeholder information desires. LISAS categorizes user requirements into six interdependent functional layers built upon large-scale cadastral base mapping ($\geq 1:5,000$), as detailed in Table [1](#bookmark=id.ewa32do3mtth) and Figure 2\.

*Table 1: Grouping of User Requirements and Layer Specifications*

| Ownership Layer | Spatial Layer | Legal & Admin | Economic & Use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Occupier Name | Large-scale Cadastral Maps | Adjudication Reports | Assessed Land Value |
| Address & Contact | Parcel Location / Coords | Subdivision Reports | Ground Rent Fees |
| Gender & Marital Status | Individual Survey Plan | Surveyor-General Approval | Mortgage Status |
| Occupation | Master / Layout Plans | Land Allocation Details | Leases / Subleases |
| Inheritance Details | Parcel Area / Boundary | Certificate of Occupancy | Current Land Use |

**2.2.1	Maps**

These are large scale cadastral maps and survey plans with identified coordinates on a geometric grid to define the parcel location in space. A base map covering the state is required in the proposed system. An approved survey plan will be entered into the system with a unique numeric identifier and information such as the name of the Registered Surveyor, date of approval and registration status in the deeds registry. A parcel identifier links the maps with the documents and survey plans as presented in Figure 2\. 

Figure 2: Parcel identifier

**2.2.2	Ownership**

Land Use Act (LUA) describes land owner as occupier (Atilola, 2010). Thus, ownership refers to right of occupation (legal and just claim with respect to the LUA) rather that right of possession. Ownership information will contain information about the occupier. From the users’ requirements survey, such information would include: name, occupation, gender, and marital status.

**2.2.3	Documents**

These are written instrument of ownership or obligation in form of a deed, mortgage or lease. All documents entered into the system would be given a unique numeric identifier and classified appropriately. Examples of such information are: file number, grantor and grantee, lessor and lessee, mortgagor and mortgagee, date of approval of C. of O., date of registration, survey plan number, payment information, (e.g. receipt number) and other registration particulars. 

**2.2.4	Valuation**

This is an appraisal of the value of a parcel and developments on the parcel at a given point in time. The category of the parcel (urban or rural), and the date of assessment are important information for valuation. The valuation is necessary for assignment, mortgage, transfer of possession, sublease, etc. The LUA prohibits the alienation of statutory right of occupancy without the consent of the State Governor. 

**2.2.5	Taxes**

The taxes such as property tax, capital gain tax, and stamp duties are normally based on the assessed value of the parcel (including the developments – property). The information will include: tax code or tax key numbers, exemption status (e.g. state property may be exempted), assessed value, postal address for tax bill and deadlines for annual property tax.

**2.2.6	Bills and payments**

This is an inbuilt control mechanism to check and record payments. The unit responsible for bills and payment will develop pricing policies and fix prices. The Bills and Payment is proposed to record and check all records relating to payments. It will confirm payments and cross-checks the information in the Taxes database.

## **2.3	Functional Specifications**

The functional specifications governing the LISAS platform include:

1. **Access Control & Authentication:** Role-based identity verification securing owner profile management and query actions.

2. **Interactive WebGIS Mapping:** Vector rendering, pan/zoom tools, land-use filtering, and parcel highlight on spatial selection.

3. **Spatial Data Management:** Storage and streaming of spatial layers, boundary survey plans, and associated attribute metadata.

4. **Multi-User Concurrency:** Simultaneous read/query client support backed by spatial database connection pooling.

5. **Standards Compliance & Scalability:** Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) compliance, extensible API hooks, and seamless extensibility.

## **2.4	Data Modeling: ISO 19152 (LADM) and Cadastre 2014/2034 Integration**

LISAS adopts the Land Administration Domain Model (ISO 19152\) and incorporates Cadastre 2014/2034 principles (**Kaufmann, 1998**; **Luthy, 2015**; **vanOosterom, 2025**). The model captures land-people relationships in accordance with the Nigerian Land Use Act (LUA) of 1978, which vests land in State Governors and restricts private tenure to a Right of Occupancy (holdings categorized as *Occupier* rights rather than absolute fee-simple ownership) (**Atilola, 2010**).

Figure [3](#bookmark=id.it0sdw78v24g) presents the UML class diagram governing the system’s object-oriented spatial data structure. 

In this spatial object model:

* **Parcel** represents the spatial polygon unit (inheriting geometry attributes from *Feature*). Cardinality relationships require a 1:1 match with **Taxes** and **Valuation**, while establishing a many-to-many (\*...\*) mapping with cadastral **SurveyPlan** records.

* **Ownership** inherits from *Object* and establishes the administrative-legal right (*Right of Occupancy*) connecting legal occupiers to registered **Document** instances (e.g., Certificate of Occupancy, Deed of Transfer, Leasehold).

# **3	Methodology and Implementation**

## **3.1	Study Area and Spatial Dataset**

The empirical test environment utilizes cadastral spatial data covering the \*\*Otedola Estate Layout\*\* located in Ojodu/Isheri, Ikeja Local Government Area, Lagos State, Nigeria. Boundary corner coordinates for 471 individual property parcels were obtained from the Office of the State Surveyor-General (OSSG), Lagos State. The geographical extent of Lagos State along with the location of Otedola Estate is depicted in Figure [4](#bookmark=id.eshfi5yoeyua).

*Figure 4: Spatial Location Context of Lagos State and Otedola Estate Layout.*

Initial AutoCAD DWG corner coordinates were transformed into ESRI Shapefile format in ArcMap/QGIS, projected to EPSG:26331 (Minna Datum / UTM Zone 31N), and uploaded to the PostGIS spatial database engine.

## **3.2	Production Three-Tier Stack Implementation**

The implementation decouples data storage, business API routing, and interactive visualization:

1. **Data Tier (PostgreSQL / PostGIS):** Persists spatial parcel geometries alongside relational attribute tables. Listing 1 details the PostGIS table definitions and spatial indexing setup.

2. **Application Tier (Python FastAPI REST Engine):** Executes spatial SQL queries, transforms coordinate projections to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and serves GeoJSON payload endpoints asynchronously. Listing 2 presents the API service implementation.

3. **Presentation Tier (Leaflet.js Web Client):** Renders dynamic tile basemaps (OpenStreetMap), parses GeoJSON spatial structures, handles user queries, and displays parcel popups.

## **3.3	Research Design and Statistical Benchmarking**

This research applies a Design Science Research (DSR) framework combined with empirical quantitative testing. Performance latency and system usability were evaluated across three test scenarios (Table [2](#bookmark=id.nmurd445fri0)), repeated for 30 cycles ($N=30$) to achieve statistical reliability.

*Table 2: System Performance Experimental Test Scenarios*

| Scenario | Operational Task | Technical Execution Path |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| S1 | Parcel Search by Identifier (ParcelID) | Exact string indexed lookup via FastAPI to PostGIS, returning GeoJSON highlight bounds. |
| S2 | Full Map Layer Load | Full vector dataset rendering (471 parcels) over OpenStreetMap basemap tiles. |
| S3 | Attribute Spatial Query | Point-in-polygon spatial click selection triggering attribute popup card rendering. |

Quantitative metrics include Variance (${\sigma }^{2}$), Coefficient of Variation ($CV$), paired-sample $t$\-tests (comparing LISAS against legacy manual bureau retrieval times), and one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) ($\alpha =0.05$). Qualitative usability was measured using the standardized System Usability Scale (SUS) 10-item instrument.

$${\sigma }^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\mu {)}^{2}$$

$$CV=\left({\frac{\sigma }{\mu }}\right)\times 100%$$

# **4	Results**

## **4.1	Interface Functionality and Operational Workflow**

The implemented LISAS interface provides a web portal for land information access:

1. **Authentication Portal:** Users authenticate using registered credentials and assigned Parcel Identifiers. Successful authentication generates a personalized dashboard displaying user profiles, parcel spatial extent, land-use classifications, and area calculations.

2. **Interactive Map Canvas:** The main interface presents a Leaflet.js map equipped with layer control toggles, an exact-string Parcel ID search engine, land-use dropdown filters (Residential, Commercial, Industrial), spatial GeoJSON editing tools, PDF map export functions, and CSV attribute extract utilities.

3. **Interactive Attribute Popups:** Clicking a parcel feature triggers an spatial attribute popup card displaying the ParcelID, Owner Name, Tax ID, Survey Plan Number, Date of Birth, and calculated area.

## **4.2	System Latency and Execution Performance**

System latency benchmarks across the 30 repeated execution cycles are summarized in Table [3](#bookmark=id.do1q6cfw2ddt).

*Table 3: Quantitative Performance Benchmark Results ($N=30$)*

| Metric / Operation | Mean ($\mu $) | Std. Dev ($\sigma $) | Variance (${\sigma }^{2}$) | CV (%) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| S1: Parcel Search Time | 0.82 s | 0.15 s | 0.0225 | 18.29% |
| S2: Map Load Time | 1.94 s | 0.30 s | 0.0900 | 15.46% |
| S3: Query Response Time | 0.65 s | 0.12 s | 0.0144 | 18.46% |

All operations achieved execution times well within acceptable WebGIS responsiveness limits ($<2.0$ seconds). Lightweight spatial attribute queries (S3) and indexed string searches (S1) performed fastest ($\mu =0.65$ s and $\mu =0.82$ s, respectively). Map layer rendering (S2) exhibited the highest mean load time ($\mu =1.94$ s) due to client-side vector polygon drawing over network tile streams.

## **4.3	Comparative Analysis with Legacy Systems**

Comparative evaluation between traditional manual physical bureau searching and digital LISAS operations reveals significant time savings (Table [4](#bookmark=id.pvorxotl4f0x)).

*Table 4: Comparative Efficiency Analysis: Manual Bureau vs. LISAS Platform*

| Operational Task | Traditional Bureau | LISAS Platform | Performance Gain |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Parcel Boundary Search | 15 – 30 minutes | 0.82 seconds | $>99%$ Faster |
| Attribute Data Retrieval | Manual Paper Search | Instant Popup Click | Real-time Access |
| Public Accessibility | Physical Bureau Visit | Web Browser Access | 24/7 Portal |

A paired-sample $t$\-test yielded $t=18.72$ ($p=0.001<0.05$), confirming a statistically significant reduction in processing time. One-way ANOVA testing across operational scenarios resulted in $F=6.45$ ($p=0.002$), reflecting expected computational variance between lightweight database querying and heavier browser map graphic rendering.

## **4.4	Usability Evaluation (SUS Score)**

Assessment via the System Usability Scale (SUS) yielded a mean usability score of 82.5 / 100, placing LISAS in the "Grade A / Excellent" usability category. Correlation analysis between user SUS evaluation scores and task completion times produced a strong negative correlation coefficient ($r=-0.68,p<0.01$), indicating that the intuitive WebGIS interface directly reduces operational task duration.

## **4.5	Statistical Distribution and Performance Convergence**

Figure 5 illustrates the statistical distribution of system response times alongside convergence performance curves over repeated iterations.

*Figure 8: System Performance Distribution (a) Boxplots showing median and interquartile* 

*ranges, and (b) Response time convergence curves over 30 test iterations.*

The low spread in boxplots for S1 and S3 demonstrates operational stability. All convergence curves stabilize rapidly beyond 15 iterations, confirming the statistical reliability and reproducibility of the measurements.

The **parcel search and query operations** show **lower median values and smaller IQR**, indicating faster response times, high consistency and stability. The **map load operation** exhibits a **higher median response time and a wider spread (larger IQR).** This suggests that map rendering is more computationally intensive and sensitive to factors such as data size and browser performance. The system performs **most efficiently for lightweight operations** (search and query). **Map loading is the primary performance bottleneck**, which is typical in WebGIS systems due to rendering of multiple geometries and client-side processing. The relatively **tight clustering of values** (few or no extreme outliers) indicates **stable system performance**, which is desirable for real-world deployment.

Each curve in Figure 8 (b) represents the **cumulative mean response time** for search, map load, and query. The x-axis represents the **number of test iterations**, while the y-axis shows the **average response time (seconds)**. 

The **search and query curves stabilize quickly**, showing low variability and high predictability. The **map load curve stabilizes more slowly**, reflecting higher computational demand, and greater variability in execution time. 

The convergence behavior can be seen in the fact that all curves gradually **stabilize as the number of iterations increases**. This indicates that the system produces **consistent results over time, and p**erformance measurements are **reliable and reproducible.** The convergence of curves also confirms the **statistical reliability of the experimental results**. The stability suggests that LISAS is suitable for **consistent real-world use**. The slower convergence of map loading highlights the need for optimization techniques such as tile-based rendering, server-side processing, spatial indexing. 

As shown in Tabe 5, all operations show **CV \< 20%**, which indicates **good consistency, and acceptable performance reliability.** Despite higher absolute variance**, map load has a slightly lower CV**, meaning variability is proportional to its higher mean, and performance is still relatively stable in context. 

Table 5: Correlative variability interpretation based on statistical analysis results

| Operation | Mean (s) | Std Dev | CV (%) | Interpretation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Query | 0.65 | 0.12 | \~18% | Highly stable |
| Search | 0.82 | 0.15 | \~18% | Stable |
| Map Load | 1.94 | 0.30 | \~15% | Moderate variability |

The **smooth convergence of curves** indicates decreasing variance over iterations and stabilization of mean. As *number of iterations* tends to infinity, $mean$ stabilizes, and $standard\ deviation$ reduces influence of random fluctuations. This confirms **statistical reliability of measurements.** 

# **5	Discussion**

The implementation and performance evaluation of LISAS provide concrete empirical evidence of the transformative impact of WebGIS architectures on urban land information service delivery. By transitioning land data retrieval from legacy manual registry searches to an online geospatial interface, the platform reduces query latency by over 99% (from 15–30 minutes down to sub-second responses). This sharp efficiency improvement aligns with findings in recent land administration literature emphasizing the necessity of digital service delivery for modern land governance (**Adam, 2023**; **Rohan, 2023**).

Statistically, the tight clustering of response times (${\mu }_{search}=0.82$ s, ${\mu }_{query}=0.65$ s) and low Coefficients of Variation ($CV<20%$) confirm that decoupled client/server WebGIS platforms achieve reliable operational stability. Map load rendering represented the single largest latency component ($\mu =1.94$ s), which is typical for browser-based vector polygon rendering over web mapping APIs (**Luong, 2025**). The rapid convergence of performance curves (Figure [5](#bookmark=id.z9x8cc3ufz8a)b) validates the statistical consistency of the benchmarking methodology.

Furthermore, achieving a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of \*\*82.5\*\* demonstrates high public acceptability. This usability result is notable within African developing contexts, where low digital literacy often poses adoption hurdles (**Duku, 2023**). The strong negative correlation ($r=-0.68$) between usability score and task duration confirms that intuitive user interface design directly improves user task performance.

# **6	Conclusion and Recommendations**

This study presented the technical design, enterprise data modeling, implementation, and statistical evaluation of LISAS, a modern WebGIS interface for parcel information services in Lagos State. The system successfully demonstrates how open-source geospatial tools—specifically PostgreSQL/PostGIS, FastAPI REST services, and Leaflet.js—can be combined to build a lightweight, high-performance, and cost-effective digital parcel access portal. Empirical benchmark results validate that the platform delivers sub-second response times, statistically significant efficiency gains over traditional manual processes ($p<0.001$), and high user acceptance (82.5 SUS).

While LISAS provides a robust spatial platform for parcel visualization and attribute retrieval, transitioning the system into a full statewide Land Information System across Lagos State requires key future technical enhancements:

1. **Transition to Vector Tiles (MVT):** For statewide deployments containing hundreds of thousands of cadastral parcels, static GeoJSON payloads should be replaced with Mapbox Vector Tiles (.pbf) served dynamically via GeoServer or Martin tile engines to maintain fast rendering speeds.

2. **OAuth2 / OpenID Connect Security:** Implement role-based token authentication to protect sensitive owner data and restrict administrative editing endpoints.

3. **Full Workflow Automation:** Expand backend API services to support automated land title verification, survey plan boundary checking algorithms, encumbrance tracking, and electronic document submission.

4. **Interoperable Spatial Standards:** Expose OGC-compliant Web Feature Services (WFS) and Web Map Services (WMS) endpoints to enable interoperability across Lagos State Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs).

In conclusion, the LISAS platform offers a scalable, fit-for-purpose technical framework that advances digital land administration in Nigeria and provides a repeatable model for similar developing regions.
